Translator's note: the original title of this essay is An Appeal for the Restoration of the Life-Releasing Pond at Jile Temple, Nanxun. For ease of circulation and recitation, it is abbreviated as “The Essay on Releasing Living Beings”

The act of refraining from killing and releasing living beings is plain and easy to see; the principle behind it is profound and hard to fathom. If one does not understand the principle, then even if one can perform the act, one's heart can never be wholly sincere and compassionate, and the blessings of one's merit will shrink to meagerness in proportion to the narrowness of one's mind. Should one meet with the obstruction and slander of the ignorant, one may be swayed by them, and a heart full of goodwill may be snuffed out on the spot. For this reason I do not shrink from many words, but set forth the principle at length: that all creatures may together bathe in compassionate grace, and that human beings may each cultivate their own blessings; that through deep and heartfelt benevolence we may extinguish the killing retribution of self and other, together reach the realm of long life, and share in the joy of our natural years. May this merit further be dedicated toward the Western Land. Then we shall forever leave the cycle of birth and death, rise far above the three realms, become disciples of Amitabha, and be good companions among the ocean-wide assembly. May the reader take heed.

To begin with, the one-thought mind-nature of all beings of water and land is in no way different from that of the Buddhas of the three times. It is only because the power of past evil karma veils the wondrous brightness that it cannot manifest, and so they have sunk into the other kinds of existence. As a result their knowledge is crude and meager; apart from seeking food and fleeing death, they know nothing at all. It is like a great bronze mirror of priceless worth that has lain covered in dust for kalpas. Not only is there no brightness whatsoever, but even the bronze body itself does not show, so that it is no better than a piece of rubbish. If one day it meets a wise man who recognizes it as a precious mirror possessing boundless light that illumines heaven and earth, and who then polishes it day after day, at first the mirror's body faintly shows, and next its light gradually shines forth. When the polishing reaches its utmost, the light that illumines heaven and earth is revealed in its entirety. Only then does the unwise man come to prize it, regarding it as a supreme treasure. One should know that this light belongs to the mirror from the start and is not gained through polishing. Yet although it is inherent, without the condition of polishing, from kalpa to kalpa there would never be a day when it shone.

The mind-nature of all beings in the six paths, human and heavenly alike, is entirely the same. From time without beginning it has been veiled by delusion and karma, so that its inherent wondrous brightness cannot shine forth; they turn their backs on the true nature and create the karma of birth and death. The Greatly Enlightened World-Honored One, knowing that the one-thought mind-nature of all beings is of the same kind as the Buddha's, employed all manner of skillful means and taught the Dharma according to each one's capacity. He universally bade them cultivate the path of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, hoping thereby to cut off delusion and karma and recover what is originally theirs, to perfect blessings and wisdom and realize the dharmakāya. He further bade the people of the world arouse the mind of compassion, refrain from killing, and release living beings. This is because I and all living beings are alike within the cycle of birth and death. From time without beginning we have in turn given birth to one another and in turn killed one another. Each of them has been my father or mother, my brother or sister, my son or daughter; and I likewise have been father or mother, brother or sister, son or daughter to each of them. Through the power of evil karma, they have repeatedly suffered slaughter at my hands, whether as humans or as other kinds of beings; and through the power of evil karma, I too have suffered slaughter at their hands, whether as a human or as another kind of being. Across long kalpas we have slain and been born to one another without end. Ordinary beings do not know this, but the Tathāgata sees it with utter clarity. Not to reflect on it is one thing, but to reflect on it is to feel boundless shame and compassion!

Now, through the blessings and good deeds of past lives, I have been fortunate enough to be born in the human realm. Surely I should untie grudges and dissolve enmity, refrain from killing and release living beings, so that every creature that has life may dwell where it belongs. I should further recite the Buddha's name on their behalf and dedicate the merit to the Pure Land, so that they may be delivered. Even if their karma is heavy and they cannot be reborn at once, by relying on this merit of compassion and goodness I shall resolutely pray that at life's end I be reborn in the Western Land. Once reborn there, I shall rise beyond the ordinary to the holy, end birth and death, forever leave the cycle of transmigration, and gradually realize the fruit of Buddhahood.

Moreover, cherishing living things and releasing them is something the sages and worthies of old all practiced. Thus the Book of Documents contains the words, “Let the birds, beasts, fish, and turtles all follow their nature,” and King Wen's benevolence reached even to dried bones — how much more to creatures possessed of perception! As for Jianzi releasing the turtle-doves, Zichan keeping fish, the Marquis of Sui aiding the snake, and Yang Bao rescuing the sparrow — these were the hearts of sages who regarded all with equal benevolence. Yet even they did not yet know that all wriggling creatures with sentience possess the Buddha-nature, that humans and animals rise and fall in turn and are by turns enemy and kin, and that they are destined in the end to attain Buddhahood. Only when the great teaching came east did the principles of the cause and effect of the three times and of the equal, undifferentiated mind-nature of living beings and Buddhas shine forth clearly in the world. Henceforth every great sage and worthy made refraining from killing and releasing living beings the foundation for averting the calamity of slaughter, cultivating the fruit of blessings, stilling the clash of arms, and enjoying one's natural years in peace.

The ancients said: “If you would know the calamity of swords and spears in the world, listen to the sound that rises from the slaughterhouse at midnight.” They also said: “If you would have a world without the calamity of arms, there is no way but for beings to abstain from eating flesh.” From this we know that refraining from killing and releasing living beings is the excellent plan that pulls out the root and stops up the source in saving the world. Thus Master Zhiyi bought more than sixty places along the rivers and estuaries by the sea, stretching over four hundred li, to serve as life-releasing ponds. He petitioned for an imperial edict to erect a stele forbidding fishing; those who secretly fished invariably met with misfortune. This remained so down to the Zhenguan reign of the Tang. In the second year of the Qianyuan reign of Emperor Suzong of Tang, an edict was issued commanding every prefecture to establish life-releasing ponds, and Yan Zhenqing was commanded to compose the stele inscription and to write it in red. Part of it reads: “Our emperor takes the whole world as a pond, so that all within the realm may receive blessings; relying on the power of the dhāraṇī's empowerment, the ford of birth and death in the sea of afflictions is exhausted. Measured against antiquity, how could anything compare?” In the first year of the Tianxi reign of Emperor Zhenzong of Song, an edict commanded the establishment of life-releasing ponds throughout the land, and West Lake in Hangzhou was likewise a life-releasing pond of the Song. In the Ming dynasty, Master Lianchi established life-releasing ponds at Shangfang and Changshou. His Essay on Refraining from Killing and Releasing Living Beings circulated throughout the world. In the three hundred and more years since, the monks and laypeople who have looked up to his lofty example and compassionately aided living creatures are beyond all counting.

Someone may ask: widowers, widows, orphans, and the childless, the poor and the afflicted, are to be found everywhere — why not relieve them, instead of busying oneself so earnestly with other kinds of beings to which one has no relation? Is this not to invert what is urgent and what is trivial, what is weighty and what is light?

I answer: you do not yet know the reason the Tathāgata teaches people to refrain from killing and to release living beings. Although humans and animals differ, the Buddha-nature is originally the same. They have sunk into other kinds of existence through evil karma, while we have been fortunate to gain human form through good karma. If we do not show them pity but eat their flesh to our heart's content, then the moment our blessings run out and their offenses come to an end, we cannot avoid repaying them in full and filling their mouths in turn. Know that the great calamity of swords and spears is all elicited by the killing karma of past lives. If there is no killing karma, then even should one encounter bandits, they will give rise to goodwill and not take one's life. What is more, those who refrain from killing and release living beings rarely meet with pestilence, flood, fire, and other sudden disasters. From this we know that protecting life is in truth protecting oneself. Refraining from killing can avert death by heaven, by ghosts and spirits, by robbers, and by the mutual vengeance of enemies in the future. As for widowers, widows, orphans, the childless, the poor, and the afflicted, one should likewise relieve them to the best of one's ability. How could those who refrain from killing and release living beings fail to perform this merit at all? Yet although the widowed and orphaned are deeply pitiable, they have not yet reached the point of death, whereas an animal, if not ransomed at once, will be seen cooked in the pot to fill someone's belly.
Again someone asks: living creatures are without limit — how many can one release?

I answer: one should know that releasing living beings is in truth the finest way of rousing in all people the most excellent good heart of universally protecting life. It is hoped that they will grasp the intent of releasing beings, feel a stirring of pity within, and be unable to bear eating them. Since none eat them, those who catch them will cease. Then all creatures of water, land, and air will freely fly, walk, and swim within the realms where they themselves move, and this becomes a universal release without any act of releasing. Is this not what is meant by “taking the whole world as a pond”? Even if not every person can be like this, yet if a single person cannot bear to eat meat, then countless lives of water and land are spared from slaughter — how much more when it is not only one person! Moreover, this severs for all our companions, present and future, the causes of widowhood, orphanhood, loneliness, childlessness, poverty, and affliction, and it creates for them the conditions of long life without illness, wealth and honor and ease, the reunion of fathers and sons, and of husbands and wives growing old together. It is precisely a way of relieving in advance, so that in lives to come, age after age, they may never meet with the miseries of widowhood and orphanhood and the like, but long enjoy the happiness of long life and prosperity. Is this not what is meant by “all within the realm receiving blessings”? How can one set it aside with indifference? Think it over carefully: in refraining from killing and releasing living beings, is one in the end busying oneself earnestly for people, or busying oneself earnestly for animals, and inverting what is urgent and trivial, weighty and light?

Outside Jile Temple at Nanxun there has long been a life-releasing pond. Because its banks were not fully faced with stone, it had collapsed, and since it had not been dredged for many years, it was filled with silt. Whenever well-meaning people released living beings into the river, although they arouse a good heart, the beings they released could hardly benefit; those released in the morning and caught again by evening were in the majority. Near a great river it is indeed proper to release them into the water, but a small river is by no means suitable. Master Yuanlin, unable to bear this, planned to dredge the pond deeply and build an enclosing wall around it as protection, so that there would be a place for releasing beings and no way for them to be stolen or caught — a most generous intention. Before the work began, Master Juesan of Putuo happened to arrive, and at their first meeting they found themselves of one mind and one way. Master Yuanlin thereupon entrusted the affairs of the temple to him, and himself laid down the myriad entanglements and devoted himself solely to the Pure Land practice. Master Juesan, taking up the unfinished task, wished to complete it quickly. But the work being vast, it could not be done by one man alone, so he planned to solicit donations from the faithful of the whole town to accomplish the noble undertaking together, and he asked me to write a preface.

I have long grieved over the cruelty of the killing calamity of recent times, wishing to avert it yet lacking the strength; his request stirred my heart. So I have set down in brief the true mind originally possessed by humans and animals alike, their rising and falling according to karma, and the present and future rewards of killing and of protecting life. I hope that all you donors will together arouse good thoughts and together contribute your pure wealth, so that this undertaking may quickly be accomplished, and all creatures may each find their proper place. The merit and benefit of this are measureless and boundless. Not only will the myriad calamities of this present life melt away like ice and a thousand blessings gather like clouds, but in lives to come those who repay this kindness and virtue will be beyond counting, by the millions and billions!
Translated by Zhanran

The act of refraining from killing and releasing living beings is plain and easy to see, but the principle behind it is profound and hard to fathom. If one does not understand the principle, then even if one can carry out the act, one will never have a heart of utmost sincerity and compassion, and the blessings of one's field of merit will shrink to meagerness in proportion to the narrowness of one's mind. If one meets with the obstruction and slander of people who do not understand the principle, one may well change one's original intent, and a heart full of goodwill may be snuffed out on the spot. So here I do not shrink from a lengthy explanation, but set forth the principle of refraining from killing and releasing living beings, so that animals may together bathe in compassionate grace and human beings may each cultivate their blessings, so that through sincere, heartfelt, all-embracing love we may extinguish the killing retribution of self and other, together enjoy long life, and share the joy of our natural years. And I pray that this merit be dedicated toward rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Then we shall forever leave the cycle of birth and death, rise far above the three realms, become disciples of Amitabha Buddha, and be good friends of the pure bodhisattvas of the great sea-like assembly. May the reader read it carefully.

It is only because the evil karma of past lives veils the wondrous, bright true mind and keeps it from manifesting that they have fallen into other kinds of existence. Yet although the light is inherent in the mirror, without the condition of polishing, from kalpa to kalpa there would never be a day when it shone.

Now, having received the Buddha's instruction, I myself know this business of giving birth to and killing one another. Not to reflect on it is one thing, but to reflect on it is to feel boundless shame and compassion!

Now, through the blessings and good deeds of past lives, I have been fortunate enough to be born in the human realm. Surely I should dissolve enmity and dispel hatred, refraining from killing and releasing living beings, so that every creature that has life may dwell where it belongs. Once reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, I shall immediately rise beyond the ordinary to the holy, end birth and death, forever leave the cycle of transmigration, and gradually realize the fruit of Buddhahood.

Moreover, cherishing living things and releasing them is something the sages and worthies of old all practiced. Thus the Book of Documents contains the words, “Let the birds, beasts, fish, and turtles all follow their nature (that is, let them all follow their innate nature, so that they do not suffer the pain of being killed or the terror of being startled and driven into flight),” and King Wen's benevolence reached even to dried bones — how much more to animals possessed of perception! Thereafter every great sage and worthy made refraining from killing and releasing living beings the foundation for averting the calamity of slaughter, cultivating the fruit of blessings, stilling the clash of arms, and enjoying one's natural years in peace.

[Jianzi releases the turtle-doves] This is a story of the Warring States period, in which the feudal lord Zhao Jianzi released turtle-doves: on New Year's Day (the first day of the first month), a man of Handan presented turtle-doves to Zhao Jianzi. Zhao Jianzi was delighted and rewarded him generously. A guest asked him why he was so pleased, and Zhao Jianzi replied: “I can release them, to show my benevolence and kindness.” The guest said: “When everyone learns that you wish to release living beings, they will cater to your wishes and vie to catch them for you to release. With all this catching and releasing, many will die or be injured. If you truly do not wish to harm them, the best course is to forbid catching them. If they are caught only to be released again, your kindness will not make up for your fault.” Zhao Jianzi gladly adopted this advice and issued an order strictly forbidding their capture. [Zichan keeps fish] Someone presented fish to Zichan (a disciple of Confucius), and, unable to bear having them killed, he put them all into a pond. [The Marquis of Sui aids the snake] When the Marquis of Sui was traveling to the state of Qi, he saw a snake trapped on a sandbank, its head bleeding. He lifted it up with his staff and placed it in the water. On his return he passed the place again, and the snake presented him with a precious pearl held in its mouth. [Yang Bao rescues the sparrow] When Yang Bao was young, he saw a yellow sparrow that had been struck down by an owl and lay wounded on the ground, hemmed in on all sides by ants. He picked up the yellow bird, carried it home, put it in a box, and fed it with yellow flowers. When its wound healed, he released it to fly away. That night he dreamed that a boy in yellow robes came to thank him and gave him four jade rings, saying: “I am an envoy of the Queen Mother of the West, and I owe my life to your rescue. Your descendants will all be of lofty virtue and unblemished integrity, enjoying wealth, honor, and glory, ranked among the three highest ministers, just like these four jade rings.” Afterwards, Yang Bao's descendants flourished in high office for four generations.

The ancients said: “If you would know the calamity of swords and spears in the world, listen to the sound that rises from the slaughterhouse at midnight.” They also said: “If you would have a world without the calamity of arms, there is no way but for beings to abstain from eating flesh.” From this we know that refraining from killing and releasing living beings is the good method that saves people at the very root. He further petitioned the court to issue an order erecting a stele forbidding fishing, with severe punishment for any who fished secretly. This remained so down to the Zhenguan reign of the Tang. Looking back over the dynasties, how could any achievement compare with this?”
